dossier:
There is a beautiful, stubborn absurdity to New Zealand's place in football history. They are the only team to leave a World Cup entirely unbeaten — three draws against Slovakia, Italy, and Paraguay in South Africa in 2010 — and still fly home early. No wins, no losses, just three shrugs from a nation that was supposed to be cannon fodder and refused to play along. That story alone earns them a seat at any table.

The All Whites carry a chip on their shoulder the size of the Southern Alps. Ranked 83rd in the world, they qualify through OFC, a confederation so small and isolated that critics sniff they haven't truly been tested. But that disrespect is fuel. This is a squad that scraps, organizes, and believes, built around players who have carved out real careers in Europe — not passengers, but workers who know exactly what underdog football demands of them.

For 2026, the dream is simple: win one. Just one. Chris Wood brings Premier League pedigree and the kind of physical menace that can unsettle any defence on a given day. Marko Stamenic brings midfield craft. Liberato Cacace brings electric energy down the flank. The pieces are there. The hunger is undeniable. Whether the tournament gods are kind enough to give them the moment — well, that's always the question, isn't it.
whatToWatch: Watch New Zealand for the sheer joy of a team that has absolutely nothing to lose and genuinely does not care who is standing in their way. If Wood gets a sniff at goal in front of a packed stadium, the noise from a tiny footballing nation echoing around North America will be something you will not forget.
xFactor: Liberato Cacace — the Empoli wing-back has the pace and directness to terrorize opposition fullbacks and turn half-chances into genuine crises for anyone unlucky enough to face him.
verdict: New Zealand will arrive as everyone's second-favourite team, play with the fearlessness of people who have already beaten the odds just by being there, and make at least one much bigger nation deeply uncomfortable.
funFacts: New Zealand's 1-1 draw with Italy in 2010 remains one of the great upsets in World Cup group stage history — the Azzurri were defending champions at the time.
The All Whites had to wait 28 years between their first World Cup appearance in 1982 and their return in 2010, a gap that makes their unbeaten record feel even more remarkable.
name: New Zealand
